notesStmt.note: This is one of many similar corrected proof slips of this poem. Horace Traubel includes a facsimile of a nearly identical slip in With Walt Whitman in Camden and notes that although Whitman was in the practice of having poems "set up for private distribution [i.e., to friends and admirers] at the printing office of Henry Curtz," he never gave out the slips until the poems had been published ([Boston: Small, Maynard & Company, 1906] 1:180). As the text of the poem in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891) bears several alterations not present here, this proof slip probably dates to shortly after the poem's first appearance in 1887. An image of the verso is unavailable.

This is a proof slip, with a correction in Whitman's hand, for "Shakspere-Bacon's Cipher," which first appeared in The Cosmopolitan magazine in October 1887, where it was titled "Shakspere Bacon's Cipher." It was reprinted in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891) under the title "Shakspere-Bacon's Cipher."

lg.head: SHAKSPERE-BACON'S CIPHER.
(A Hint to Scientists.)
lg.l: I doubt it not––then more, far more;
In each old song bequeath'd––in every noble page or text,

In every object, mountain, tree, and star—in every birth and
life,

As part of each––finality of each—meaning, behind the os-
